scenes.heading: sync: Mutex, RWMutex & WaitGroup
scenes.narration: Let's look at the sync package: Mutex, RWMutex, and WaitGroup, the tools that protect shared state across goroutines.

scenes.heading: Three primitives, three jobs
items: Mutex: one goroutine in the critical section at a time
RWMutex: many readers OR one writer
WaitGroup: wait for a set of goroutines to finish
A data race is undefined behavior — always synchronize
scenes.narration: The sync package guards shared memory with three primitives. A Mutex gives one goroutine exclusive access to a critical section while others block at the door. An RWMutex relaxes that, allowing many concurrent readers or a single exclusive writer. A WaitGroup is a counter that lets you wait for a group of goroutines to finish. Whenever goroutines write shared memory without synchronization, you get a data race, which is undefined behavior.

scenes.heading: How a Mutex serializes goroutines
steps: G1 calls Lock and enters the section
G2 calls Lock but the lock is held, so it parks
G1 safely reads-modifies-writes the shared state
G1 calls Unlock, waking a waiter
G2 acquires the lock and proceeds
scenes.narration: Picture two goroutines contending for one lock. Goroutine one calls Lock and enters the critical section; the lock is now held. Goroutine two calls Lock, but since it's taken, the runtime parks it off the run queue instead of spinning. Goroutine one safely reads, modifies, and writes the shared counter, then calls Unlock, which wakes a waiter. Now goroutine two acquires the lock and runs. The increments are serialized, so no race and a correct total.

scenes.heading: A concurrency-safe counter
scenes.narration: Here everything comes together. The Counter embeds a Mutex; Inc locks, defers the Unlock so it's released on every path, and increments inside the critical section. In main we call Add before launching each goroutine, defer Done inside, and Wait blocks until all one hundred finish. Note the pointer: we pass a star Counter so the lock is never copied. The result is exactly one hundred, race-free.

scenes.text: Mutexes are not reentrant and must never be copied — use pointer receivers and defer Unlock.
scenes.narration: Two rules save you from painful bugs. Go's Mutex is not reentrant, so a goroutine that locks and then calls another method that locks the same mutex deadlocks itself. And a lock must never be copied after use, since copying duplicates its internal state and breaks exclusion. Use pointer receivers, always defer your Unlock, and let go vet catch lock copies for you.
